o: Starting from an all-zero string s, each operation flips the entire suffix beginning at some index i, and we need the fewest operations to reach target. In example 1, target = "10111": flip at index 2 to get "00111", flip at 0 to get "11000", flip at 1 to get "10111" — three operations, matching the expected output. The crucial observation is that position i’s current value depends only on the PARITY of how many flips started at indices <= i, not on which ones they were. So a single left-to-right scan with one parity bit suffices: whenever target[i] disagrees with the effective (possibly flipped) bit, we are forced to start a new operation exactly at i.
k: A suffix flip toggles everything after its start, so scanning left to right only the running flip parity matters.
Every mismatch between target[i] and the effective bit forces a new operation, which immediately fixes that position.
Equivalently the answer is (target[0] == "1") plus the number of adjacent positions where target changes value.

a.i: Maintain the working string explicitly; at each position compare with target and on mismatch physically flip the whole remaining suffix while counting an operation. This mirrors the operations literally and is easy to trust, but costs quadratic time on adversarial inputs such as alternating targets.
s: Initialize s as an array of n zeros.
Scan i from left to right.
If s[i] differs from target[i], invert every character of s[i..n-1] and add 1 to ops.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — up to n operations each rewriting a suffix of length up to n.
a.sp: O(n) — an explicit copy of the string.

a.i: Replace the physical suffix flips with a single flipped flag. The effective bit at position i is target-independent: it equals the original zero XOR flipped. If the wanted bit disagrees with the effective bit, one new suffix flip starting exactly here is unavoidable AND sufficient — increment the counter and toggle the flag. Each position is decided once, so this is linear.
s: For each character, let bit be its numeric value.
If bit XOR flipped is 1, increment ops and toggle flipped.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per character.

w: State the parity insight immediately; simulation is merely the stepping stone to it. Pitfalls: confusing suffix flips with prefix or range flips, counting maximal blocks of ones instead of value transitions (wrong under the suffix constraint — e.g., "10111" has two one-blocks but needs 3), and off-by-one handling of the first character. Edge cases: all zeros (0), all ones (1), strictly alternating strings (n). Follow-ups: generalize to arbitrary [l, r] range flips — the same transition-counting works — or output one valid sequence of operations.
